summary: This short Informational document specifies an Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) identifier for CoAP services secured with DTLS. With an ID registered, both ends can agree during the handshake that they will speak CoAP.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people meeting in a secret room first agree which language they will speak. This registers the name tag for the CoAP language.

subtitle: Registering a protocol name tag for CoAP when secured with DTLS.

tldr.problem: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) can be secured with DTLS, but when services advertise themselves using DNS and SVCB records, they need a standardized ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) identifier so clients know CoAP-over-DTLS will be spoken.
tldr.mechanism: This document registers the two-byte ALPN identifier 'co' (0x63 0x6f in hex) for CoAP services secured by DTLS. The short identifier helps avoid fragmentation of handshake messages in constrained networks like 6LoWPAN with small link-layer frames.
tldr.outcome: Both CoAP-over-TLS (already registered as 'coap') and CoAP-over-DTLS (new, 'co') can now be discovered and negotiated through standard DNS service records, enabling automatic protocol selection for constrained-network applications.

ALPN ID for CoAP over TLS

today: This Informational RFC is a CONSENSUS document from the IETF, published in March 2026. The ALPN ID 'co' is now the standard way to identify CoAP services secured with DTLS in DNS service records.

sections.title: ALPN for CoAP over DTLS
sections.content: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) allows two parties to agree on an application protocol during a TLS or DTLS handshake. CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) is a lightweight protocol for resource-constrained devices. RFC 8323 already registered coap as the ALPN ID for CoAP over TLS. This document registers a separate ID for CoAP over DTLS because it is not advisable to reuse the same ALPN ID for different transport layers.
sections.plainLanguage: ALPN is the handshake conversation where both sides agree which protocol they will use. This document officially names the protocol for CoAP when it uses DTLS security.

sections.title: The ALPN ID Registration
sections.content: For CoAP over DTLS, the ALPN ID is the two-byte sequence 0x63 0x6f, which is the ASCII string 'co'. This short value was chosen deliberately to reduce the size of the Client Hello and Server Hello messages in constrained networks such as 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4), where messages face link-layer fragmentation limits. The longer ID coap is retained for CoAP over TLS, since TLS handshakes typically have more room.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is short ('co') so it does not take up much space in messages sent over tiny networks. CoAP over TLS keeps the longer name ('coap') because it has more room.

sections.title: Service Discovery
sections.content: CoAP services can advertise themselves using SVCB and HTTPS resource records in the DNS, with an 'alpn' Service Parameter Key. A resolver or client looking up a CoAP service can see whether it is available over TLS (coap ID) or DTLS (co ID), and choose accordingly. This enables automatic protocol selection without hardcoding which transport to use. The discovery mechanism itself is defined in RFC 9460 and RFC 9953 (DNS over CoAP).
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask DNS for a CoAP service, the answer now tells you whether it uses TLS or DTLS. Your application can pick the right one automatically.
